set.rappels: 8 rappels on a single 60 m rope down the neighbouring Mile High Club line, from bolted anchors; do not rappel Beyond Redlining itself.
set.rappel_count_note: Eight rappels down Mile High Club's line on a single 60 m rope. That configuration is newer than the route: a dedicated rappel line was added alongside Mile High Club in August 2019 specifically so the descent could be done on a single 60 m rope, and the eight-station descent dates from then. Older counts from before 2019 differ (eight on a 70 m rope, or seven), so an older count disagreeing with this table describes the earlier descent, not an error. The line stays about 10-15 ft skier's left of the bolt line throughout, and you should prefer the skier's-left anchor wherever two exist, because most stations are doubled so that rappelling and climbing parties are not on the same anchor. Beyond Redlining is equipped for rappelling but its own line is explicitly not recommended: the first pitch is over 50 m, several pitches angle substantially left or right, and it requires angling rappels off single bolts where many rappels only reach the next anchor on rope stretch. Beyond Redlining's own hardware - a mid-pitch-1 bail station, a missing maillon on pitch 3 - belongs to that line and not to this one. No per-station rappel distances are known for the Mile High Club descent, and the rappel line does not follow the climbing line, so the pitch lengths are not a substitute; the figures given are nominal rather than measured.
set.descent_text: Do not rappel Beyond Redlining itself — official route beta explicitly says it is equipped for emergency use but 'not recommended' as a descent line, since the angle and pitch lengths make it a poor rap line, with angling rappels off single bolts that a single rope does not always reach. Instead, from the shared summit, descend via Mile High Club's dedicated rappel line, which works with a single 60m rope over 8 rappels: summit rap rings down through P7, P6 (face descent), a short rap on P5 to a ledge, P4 to one of two available anchors, then the tricky 'upper P3' rappel — this one is the most commonly botched: aim for a 10-ft-tall tree roughly 15 ft skier's-left of the climbing line, where a hidden intermediate P3 anchor is tucked in cedar bushes just below the station; missing it and rapping straight down the vertical face below can leave you well short of the next anchor on a single rope. Below that, a lower-P3 rap drops to a large ledge, then P2 and P1 anchors bring you to the base. The first rap station off the summit is set back roughly 8 ft south of the summit bolts and about 4 ft off the ground — easy to walk past if you're not looking for it. Saddlebag your rope on the way down to avoid dropping loose rock or gear on parties below; ledges on this face hold loose material. Because Beyond Redlining offers limited bail options low on the route, parties should carry a 70m rope if there's any real chance of needing to retreat mid-climb rather than topping out to the shared summit.

rappel_detail.pull: A rope end has jammed in a crack on the right side of this rappel, forcing the party to climb back up the other strand to free it - and the ground you would climb to reach it is loose. Watch where the ends land and pull away from the crack.
rappel_detail.notes: First rappel off the shared summit down to the P7 anchor on Mile High Club's line; single 60m rope reaches comfortably.
rappel_detail.anchor: summit rap rings, station ~8ft south of summit bolts and ~4ft off the ground
hazards: The edge below this station has cut a rope badly enough that the party had to chop it in half and retire it. The route page says the edge has since been ground down; the Beyond Redlining page still tells you exactly where to lay the rope, so treat it as live

A hard pendulum. The first-ascent advice is to lower to the large flake and walk left to the belay rather than rappelling free; a 2025 party swung hard right into a separate rock face on this rappel, on both of their visits
The nuts on these rap rings have been found loose - check them before you weight the station

Rappelling Beyond Redlining's own line is what this station exists to avoid: its first pitch is over 50 m, several pitches angle substantially left or right, and it needs angling rappels off single bolts, many of which only reach the next anchor on rope stretch
rappel_detail.station: Not on Beyond Redlining. From the shared summit, walk about 50 ft over to Mile High Club's top station: the rap rings sit back from the route's top, and the place to lay the rope is the least sharp part of the edge roughly 8 ft south of the bolts and about 4 ft off the ground. Toss just left of the crest, then angle down toward the lower anchor sitting at the foot of pitch 7. From here the whole descent stays about 10-15 ft skier's left of the bolt line, and for most pitches you can see the climbing anchors from the rap anchors.

rappel_detail.notes: A face-descent rappel down to the P6 anchor.
hazards: Dropping to the dihedral-top anchor instead is a specific, named mistake - the station you want is above and left of it
The published reason for tossing left is that parties climb directly below: keep the rope and anything you knock loose off them
rappel_detail.station: Toss the rope slightly left of the bolt line rather than straight down. Rappel the pitch-6 face, then move to a rap anchor about 10 ft skier's left and 10 ft higher than the anchor atop the dihedral pitch. Do not continue to the top of the dihedral pitch.

rappel_detail.notes: A short rappel down to a ledge at P5; source explicitly flags this one as short.
hazards: Free-hanging above a ledge, so you arrive spinning onto a stance rather than sliding onto it
rappel_detail.station: A short rappel from the pitch-5 station to an anchor on a ledge off to the side of the dihedral pitch. It is free-hanging above the ledge.

rappel_detail.notes: Drops to P4, where one of two available anchor options is used.
hazards: Most stations on this route have two anchors a few feet apart so ascending and descending parties do not share one - taking the wrong one puts you on top of climbers
Rope thrown from here lands on anyone on pitch 4 below
rappel_detail.station: Two anchors are available here; take the skier's-left one where you can, which keeps you off the climbing line.

rappel_detail.pull: A rope has been stuck in a crack pulling from the pitch-3 rap anchors; pull away from the crack. Feed the rope through the cedar bushes rather than throwing it.
rappel_detail.notes: The most commonly botched rappel on the descent — aim for a 10-ft-tall tree roughly 15 ft skier's-left of the climbing line; a hidden intermediate anchor is tucked in cedar bushes just below the visible upper-P3 station.
hazards: Do not rappel the vertical face straight down on a single rope: it does not reach the next anchors. Parties who missed the nook have ended up stranded short of the pitch-2 anchors and had to scramble across exposed ground
One party that missed it could not retrieve their rope at all - the pull angle around the intervening features made it stick and recovering it was judged unsafe
The tree the beta says will be flagged has never been flagged; years later the beta still only promises that it will be flagged soon
rappel_detail.station: The confusing one, and by a wide margin the most-reported problem on this descent. From the pitch-4 anchor, pass through cedar bushes directly below the station and rappel the low-angle upper part of pitch 3 - it is mostly walking. Aim for a tree about 10 ft tall standing roughly 15 ft skier's left of the climbing line; the intermediate anchor sits in a small recess just under that tree. Look for it right where the ground turns from slabby to vertical. You cannot see this anchor on the way up, so it cannot be scouted on the climb; parties have found chalk arrows pointing at it.

rappel_detail.notes: Continues down to a lower-P3 anchor, landing on a large ledge.
hazards: This is the vertical face the station above exists to get you onto safely; it is the ground you would be stranded above having missed the nook
rappel_detail.station: From the nook anchor, rappel the vertical section at the start of pitch 3 down to a large ledge, and set up at one of the anchors on top of pitch 2 - the skier's-left one if it is free.

hazards: Parties consistently record being surprised that the last anchor before the ground is a separate one, offset from the climbing anchor
rappel_detail.station: The station is NOT the pitch-1 climbing anchor, which is what people expect and head for. The rap anchor is about 10 ft down and 10-15 ft skier's left of the pitch-1 belay anchor.

rappel_detail.pull: Consider staying on rappel, walking back across to the belay bolt where the route starts, and pulling the rope from there.
rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel(s) via the P2 and P1 anchors bring you to the base of the route.
hazards: Do not treat the base of the route as the ground - the ledge you land on is exposed and hundreds of feet up
The gully to climber's right throws natural rockfall onto the start of the scramble; keep helmets on until you are clear of it, especially with parties above
rappel_detail.station: The last rappel reaches the base of the route. Expect the starting ledge to be quite exposed, several hundred feet off the ground.

review.single_rope: Eight rappels down the Mile High Club rap line on a single 60 m rope, per route pages and the developer's forum post; all stations in the table are 30 m or less.
review.changed: Removed the old two-60 m-rope aside from the count note, the two-rope retreat clause in the descent text and the double-rope/80 m wording in station 5's hazard; kept the 8-station single-rope table.

set.rappels: 8 rappels on a single 60 m rope (a 70 m gives more margin) down a rap line just left of the climb, from bolted anchors; do not miss the intermediate anchor partway down pitch 3.
set.rappel_count_note: Eight single-strand rappels off fixed bolted anchors, and a single 60 m rope is documented as sufficient for every one of them (a 70 m gives more margin). The one place a single rope can fail you is rap 5: if you miss the intermediate anchor in the nook below the small tree and continue down the vertical face, one rope cannot reach the next anchors, so find that nook anchor before committing. The rap line is not the climbing line - it stays roughly 3-5 m skier's left of the bolts for the whole descent, so anchors are found left of where you climbed and pulls are never plumb.
set.descent_text: Descend by rappelling the route itself, back down the same line you climbed — do not try to walk off. Eight single-strand rappels, all off bolted, fixed anchors (this is a sport-bolted line, so no natural gear or v-threads needed): rap 1 from the P7/summit anchor down to the anchor at the foot of pitch 7; the second rappel runs down the face to an anchor set left and above the dihedral; rap 3 is a short drop to a ledge-side anchor beside the dihedral; rap 4 goes to one of two anchors at the pitch 4 stance (favor the left one); rap 5 is a short, free-hanging rap off an upper-P3 anchor aimed at a ~10 ft tree left of the line, with an intermediate anchor in a nook below it; rap 6 is a vertical face rappel down lower P3 to a large ledge at the pitch 2 anchors; rap 7 drops to the pitch 1 anchor (10–15 ft left of the original belay); rap 8 finishes at the base. A single 60 m rope is enough for all 8 rappels, and a 70 m rope gives more margin. Because you rappel the entire route back to the start, many parties leave approach shoes and packs stashed at the base. Descent hazards: loose rock sitting on several of the belay ledges (manage ropes and stack carefully to avoid kicking debris onto the party below), some rope-stretch/rope-snag potential given the zigzagging (not straight-down) line of anchors, and lingering steep snow in the approach gully in spring that can complicate the walk back to the Sunrise Mine Trail after the last rappel.

rappel_detail.pull: Nothing on this descent pulls plumb, because the anchors zigzag left of the bolts. Flick the strands clear of the bolt line before pulling or they hang up on hardware.
rappel_detail.notes: Drops to the anchor at the base of pitch 7.
hazards: There is an edge right at the start. It has since been ground down, but put the rope over the least sharp part of it anyway.
Loose rock sits on several of the belay ledges on this route; stack ropes so you are not sweeping it off onto the party below.
rappel_detail.station: Rap rings set back from the summit at the top of pitch 7. The rappel runs diagonally down to the anchor at the base of pitch 7, which is the pattern for the whole descent: the rap line sits roughly 3-5 m (10-15 ft) skier's left of the bolted climbing line the entire way down.

rappel_detail.anchor: Bolted anchor left and above the dihedral
hazards: Throw the rope slightly left of the bolt line: climbers coming up are directly beneath, and rope thrown down the line takes loose rock with it.
rappel_detail.station: Rappel down the face to an anchor set about 3 m left of and 3 m above the top of the dihedral. Do not stop at the top of the dihedral itself — the anchor you want is above and left of it.

rappel_detail.anchor: Ledge-side bolted anchor beside the dihedral
hazards: Free-hanging finish onto a ledge — control the swing rather than arriving sideways.
Loose rock on the ledge.
rappel_detail.station: A short rappel to the anchor on the ledge beside the dihedral pitch. The last part of it hangs free above the ledge, so expect a spin before your feet find anything.

rappel_detail.notes: Two anchor options exist at this stance.
rappel_detail.anchor: One of two bolted anchors at the pitch 4 stance
hazards: Choosing the right-hand anchor drops your ropes onto anyone climbing, which is why the left is the published preference.
rappel_detail.station: Two anchors exist at the pitch 4 stance. Take the skier's-left one; the right-hand option puts your ropes across the climbing line.

rappel_detail.pull: On a single rope, missing the nook and continuing down the vertical face leaves you unable to reach the next anchors, so find the nook anchor before committing.
rappel_detail.notes: Short, free-hanging rappel aimed at a ~10ft tree left of the line.
hazards: Missing this station and continuing down the vertical face below it leaves a party on a single rope unable to reach the next anchors. This is the one place on the descent where a route-finding error strands you mid-face, and the route description flags it explicitly.
The cedar bushes hide both the anchor and the rope; do not rappel past on autopilot because the terrain is low-angle here.
rappel_detail.station: The station people miss, and the one that matters most. Push through the cedar bushes directly below the anchor above, rappel the low-angle upper part of pitch 3, and aim for a tree about 3 m tall standing roughly 5 m skier's left of the climbing line. The intermediate anchor sits in a small recess just under that tree.

rappel_detail.notes: Vertical face rappel down lower pitch 3.
rappel_detail.anchor: Bolted anchor at a large ledge, pitch 2 anchors
hazards: This is the steep face the previous warning is about — you are now committed below the nook.
Loose rock on the large ledge.
rappel_detail.station: From the nook anchor, down the vertical face of lower pitch 3 to the large ledge at the pitch 2 anchors. Take the left anchor if it is free.

hazards: Easy to arrive at the belay rather than the rap station and burn time traversing across on a slabby stance.
rappel_detail.station: Drops to the pitch 1 rappel anchor, which is about 3 m below and 3-5 m skier's left of the pitch 1 belay bolts — not the belay itself.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel to the ground; a single 60 m rope is enough for the whole sequence.
hazards: The base ledge is exposed above a long drop. Stay roped, walk back to the belay bolt and pull the rope from there rather than coming off the system on the ledge.
Keep helmets on: on a route this popular there is usually still a party above you when you land.
In spring the approach gully below still holds steep snow, which complicates the walk back to the Sunrise Mine Trail after the last rappel.
rappel_detail.station: Last rappel to the start of the route. The ledge you start from sits several hundred feet up and is truly exposed, so this is not a place to untie casually.

review.single_rope: A single 60 m rope does all 8 rappels on the dedicated rap line (developer added it so one 60 works); a 70 m is more comfortable.
review.changed: Removed the two-60 m-ropes recommendation and the two-rope pull line on rap 5, and the two-rope clause in descent text; made the single 60 m the stated default; table kept (all stations 30 m or less).

set.rappels: Most parties make three rappels on a single 60 m rope used doubled: about 25 m from the newer bolted anchor on the ridge crest down to the platform, then two of about 30 m down the Class 4 gully past the chockstone to its base. Some parties rappel twice and downclimb the lower gully instead.

review.single_rope: One 60 m rope was reported sufficient for the climb and the South Corner rappels; the existing 25/30/30 m single-rope table was kept.
review.changed: Removed only the sentence about a second rope; table and descent text already single-rope and left alone.

set.rappels: At least a dozen rappels along the ridge, off natural anchors and old tat; no single-rope line or per-station length is documented.
set.rappel_count_note: Roughly a dozen rappels (12-13) are described getting off gendarmes and pinnacles along Mongo Ridge, with no fixed anchors - natural gear and tat only. Individual rappel lengths are not known, and some of the rappels have been described as long, so it is not established that one 60 m rope reaches between every pair of anchors; no single-rope station list exists. A rope has been reported severed by rockfall on a marginal anchor along this stretch, so treat every anchor with suspicion and carry cord and slings to build or replace them.

review.single_rope: No source documents a single-rope descent or per-station lengths; first-ascent style accounts describe long rappels.
review.changed: Cleared the 12-row table, which carried unsourced per-station length guesses and workarounds that assumed a second line; stated plainly what is and is not known for one rope.

set.rappels: 3-4 rappels on a single 60 m rope through the ice chute (2-5 depending on conditions), from V-threads you build
set.rappel_count_note: Reported counts run from 2 to 5 rappels through the ice chute, depending on rope length and conditions: 1-3 on the upper ice step and 1-2 on the lower ice step. The four stations below are a typical single-rope sequence; the lower step can also be walked down in some conditions. Anchors are V-threads you build yourself (the Park Service asks that they not be left in place), and no per-station distances are published.
set.descent_text: Descending the Kautz is a real technical descent, not a walk-off, and involves multiple rappels through the ice chute — typically two to five depending on conditions, ice quality, and rope length. From the top of Wapowety Cleaver, parties reverse the glacier line down through crevassed terrain to the top of the ice chute, then find easier ground to climber's-left/east to belay into the chute rather than committing to team-arrest on exposed ice. The upper ice step (commonly a short pitch up to 300+ ft of AI3 alpine ice) is rappelled: the NPS route brief states this takes anywhere from one to three rappels depending on rope length, using 'Zero-Thread' ice anchors — a variant of the V-thread/Abalakov anchor chosen because it's equally strong but leaves no gear behind; there is no fixed/bolted hardware on this route, and the Park Service explicitly discourages leaving V-thread anchors in place between ascent and descent since they can melt out. Below the upper step, lower-angle snow leads to the lower ice step, typically descended with one to two more rappels on the same anchor style — so two to five rappels total through the chute is realistic for most parties on a single 60m rope, more if short-pitching. After the chute, a fast, alert traverse back toward the Rock Step is required, since this stretch sits directly under the active Kautz Ice Cliff. Climbing back up through the Rock Step itself (awkward 5th-class moves protected by fixed rope and old slings on rock anchors) returns parties to high camp; from there it's a walk/glissade down the Turtle Snowfield, back across the Nisqually or Wilson glacier crossing, and out to Paradise (or back down through Van Trump Park). A significant number of teams instead choose the 'up-and-over' option — descending the easier, non-technical Disappointment Cleaver/Muir Snowfield line from the summit to Camp Muir and Paradise — specifically to avoid re-descending the ice chute and Rock Step on tired legs, at the cost of having to haul full camping gear over the summit.

review.single_rope: One report gives 1 zero-thread rappel on the upper ice and 2 on the lower; park brief gives 1-3 upper and 1-2 lower. No per-station lengths.
review.changed: Cleared the four-row table (its 30 m lengths were not sourced), removed the fewer-with-more-ropes wording and the ropes-carried clause.

set.rappels: 3-4 rappels on a single 60 m rope through the ice chute (2-5 depending on conditions), from V-threads you build
set.rappel_count_note: Reported counts run from 2 to 5 rappels through the ice chute, depending on rope length and conditions: 1-3 on the upper ice step and 1-2 on the lower ice step. The four stations below are a typical single-rope sequence; the lower step can also be walked down in some conditions. Anchors are V-threads you build yourself (the Park Service asks that they not be left in place), and no per-station distances are published.
set.descent_text: Descent is normally either back down the Kautz Glacier itself (the way you came) or a carryover down the Disappointment Cleaver route to Paradise. On the headwall's ice steps specifically, a party on a single 60m rope can expect about three rappels plus some downclimbing to get back down through the steepest sections to the base of the ice pitches — rappel anchors on the ice steps are typically ice (V-thread/zero-thread) anchors, the modern standard, not fixed bolts — old ascent-placed threads should not be reused. Expect 1-3 rappels through the upper step and 1-2 more through the lower step. This is a snow/ice route with no permanent hardware. In marginal conditions, some parties place running belays or fix a line through the ice steps instead of full rappels, both for the descent and to assist less-experienced members. Below the headwall, the Kautz/Wilson Glacier descent back to the Turtle or out via Comet Falls involves standard roped glacier travel, not further rappelling.

review.single_rope: Same ice steps as Kautz Glacier: 1 upper plus 2 lower rappels reported; park brief 1-3 and 1-2. Lengths unpublished.
review.changed: Cleared the four-row table (unsourced), removed two-rope sentences from rappels, note and descent text.

set.rappels: About 6 short rappels, with some downclimbing, on a single 60 m rope down the South Ridge itself; clip existing stations and back up old webbing.
set.rappel_count_note: Reversing the South Ridge takes about 6 rappels with some downclimbing: a traverse skier's left to a gully, then about 4 more in a more direct line, ending back on the glacier. Stations are often slung horns in poor shape, so add a sling or cord at nearly every one and test each before weighting it. The Southeast Face is the other way down; its rappels end in a moat or bergschrund above the snowfield and no single-rope station list is documented for it, so a party on one rope should expect the ridge. Per-station distances are not published and are recorded as unknown.
set.descent_text: Three options exist, and the choice depends on party speed and whether you're continuing to Forbidden Peak. (1) Reverse the South Ridge: downclimb interspersed with numerous short, traversing rappels off fixed slings/anchors that are 'in abundance' along the ridge — a single rope is generally sufficient for these short raps, but carry extra webbing/cord to back up or replace tat, since stations are alpine-style (slung horns, chockstones, occasional old fixed gear) rather than bolted. This option is slower but avoids the moat problems of the SE Face line. (2) Descend the Southeast Face: downclimb from the summit area to the top rappel station, then make 5-6 rappels down the SE Face gully/slab system back toward the Taboo Glacier (no single-rope line is documented for this face, so one rope may not reach between stations) — the second station is on climber's left, the rest are straight down or climber's right. The crux of this option is the final rappel, where you must cross a moat/bergschrund to reach the snowfield below; this can be genuinely difficult and its condition can't be scoped from above, so the first person down need a picket, an ice axe and crampons to get out of the moat if needed. (3) Continue over the summit and descend via the Torment-Forbidden Traverse toward Forbidden Peak (sustained exposure, a 5.6 step and ~45-degree snow/ice) if that's the day's objective — this is a full traverse, not a simple descent, and commits you to exiting via Forbidden's West Ridge/Boston Basin instead of returning the way you came.

review.single_rope: South Ridge reversal: about 6 short rappels plus downclimbing; sources do not give a rope length but describe the rappels as short. SE Face single-rope line not documented.
review.changed: Cleared the SE Face table (it was the two-rope line), rewrote the count as the South Ridge single-rope descent, removed double-rope wording from note and descent text.
